oneSentence: A model whose trained numerical parameters are publicly released so others can run, inspect or adapt it, even if the training code, data or licence are not fully open.
plainExplanation:
An open-weight model is a machine-learning model whose weights have been released. Weights are the many numerical values that shape how the model turns an input into an output. In simple terms, they are the trained settings produced after learning from data.

What goes in depends on the model: text, images, audio or other data. What happens is that software loads the released weights into a model architecture, which is the design of the model, and then computes an output such as a summary, translation or prediction. What comes out is the model’s result, not a guarantee of truth.

The important point is what has been shared. If the weights are public, others can usually run the model on their own systems and often fine-tune it for new tasks. But open weights do not automatically mean the training data, source code, evaluation methods or legal rights are also open.

This is why the term is often confused with open-source AI, but they are not the same. Open source usually refers to software whose code is available under licences that allow use, study, modification and sharing. An open-weight model may release the weights while keeping other parts closed or restricting some uses.

everydayAnalogy.title: A shared camera preset
everydayAnalogy.story: A photographer publishes a preset file containing hundreds of tuned settings. Anyone with compatible editing software can load it and, if the terms allow, alter it. The file does not include the source photographs, the experiments used to tune the settings or necessarily the editing software itself. An open-weight model is similar: the tuned numerical values are available, while much of the process and material that produced them may remain unavailable.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A scoring sheet for duplicate records is small and easy to read, while real model weights can contain millions or billions of numbers and are not directly meaningful to most people. Also, a human clerk can explain a judgment in ordinary language more easily than a model can. The analogy helps with the idea of sharing trained parameters, but it does not show the scale, complexity or unpredictability of model behaviour.

visual.title: Open weights compared with fully open and fully closed release
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, a reader should be able to say that open weights means the trained parameters are released, but other parts of the system may still be closed or restricted.
visual.description: A three-column comparison. Each column shows the same five components: weights, source code, training data, training method and licence terms. Read left to right: fully closed release, open-weight release and more fully open release. Each component is marked as released, partly released or not released, making clear that open weights describes one component, not the whole AI system.

steps.label: Same system, different release choices
steps.explanation: Show that an AI system has several parts, and organisations can share some parts without sharing all of them.
steps.visualInstruction: Render three vertical panels with identical rows: Weights, Code, Data, Training method, Licence. Use consistent icons and colour states: released, partial, not released.

steps.label: Closed model
steps.explanation: In a closed release, the public may get an interface or service, but not the internal weights or other building parts.
steps.visualInstruction: In the left panel, mark all five rows as not released except optionally a small footer tag saying 'public access via service only'.

steps.label: Open-weight model
steps.explanation: Here the weights are released, so others can run the trained model. Other rows remain mixed: some may be closed, partly described or restricted.
steps.visualInstruction: In the middle panel, mark Weights as released. Mark Code, Data and Training method as partial or not released. Mark Licence as either partial or restricted with a note icon.

steps.label: More fully open release
steps.explanation: A more open release may share code and documentation too, and sometimes data, but this is a broader condition than open weights alone.
steps.visualInstruction: In the right panel, mark Weights and Code as released, Training method as released, Data as partial or released, and Licence as permissive. Add a small note: 'varies by project'.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each row to reveal a short tooltip explaining that component and why its release matters for reuse, auditing or legal permissions.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram compares three ways an AI system can be released. Each column contains the same five parts: weights, source code, training data, training method and licence terms. In the closed column, none of these parts are released to the public, though people may still use the system through an online service. In the open-weight column, the weights are released, which means others can run the trained model, but the code, data, method and licence may still be partly closed or restricted. In the more fully open column, the weights, code and method are released, and the data and licence are more open, though this varies by project. The main lesson is that 'open weights' refers only to release of trained parameters, not full openness of the whole system.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Show the same three-column comparison as a static table with colour labels and a visible legend for released, partial and not released. Tooltips are replaced by short text under each row title.

workedExample.scenario: An information management officer at a regional hub tests a publicly released summarisation model in an isolated environment before an information and communications technology governance review.
workedExample.input: Prompt: "Summarise this public 220-word meeting note in three bullet points and keep all dates unchanged."
process: The officer checks what was actually released: checkpoint files containing the trained weights, licence terms and enough format information to use a compatible runtime.
The checkpoint is downloaded from the stated source and loaded into approved software on local infrastructure. The original training data and training pipeline are not part of the release.
The software processes the meeting note using the learned parameter values in the checkpoint and generates a summary without sending the text to a hosted model service.
The officer compares the output with the source, records an altered date and notes that access to the weights does not explain which training examples produced the error.
workedExample.result: The model can be executed locally because its weights are available in a usable format. Whether it can be fine-tuned, redistributed or used operationally still depends on the licence, supporting software, technical assessment and governance clearance.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A chief of section in a procurement unit is considering whether an open-weight model could help screen a long list of vendor applications against an approved roster profile before the file moves to substantive review.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Publicly released weights could be run and tested in an approved internal environment rather than through an external service. The unit could also adapt the model if the licence permits. It would still need compatible software, adequate infrastructure and evidence that the proposed use is reliable and lawful.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Real applications, personal data and procurement-sensitive submissions must not be loaded into a model or test environment that has not been formally approved for that data and workflow. Open weights do not establish security, fairness or fitness for purpose. They also do not justify automated eligibility or ranking decisions without authorised governance and meaningful human review.

whyItMatters: The phrase affects procurement, risk assessment and governance. If weights are released, an organisation may be able to run the model itself, test it more deeply and adapt it to local needs. But that does not tell you whether the training data are known, whether the licence permits your use, or whether the system is safe, fair or suitable for sensitive work. Knowing the distinction helps avoid overclaiming transparency.
whereYouMayHearIt: A vendor demo in a procurement meeting on local hosting
An information and communications technology governance board reviewing architecture options
A technical review before clearance of a model pilot
An inter-agency working group comparing model adaptation options

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If a model is open-weight, it is open source.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Not necessarily. Open weights means the trained parameters are available. Open source usually concerns software code and the legal rights to use, study, modify and share it. A project can release weights while keeping code, data or some usage rights restricted.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If weights are public, the model is transparent enough to audit easily.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Released weights can improve access for testing, but weights are huge numerical files, not a plain-language explanation. Meaningful auditing may still require documentation, evaluation results, system prompts, safety measures, training details and information about intended and prohibited uses.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Open-weight models are automatically safer because more people can inspect them.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Broader access can support testing and independent scrutiny, but it can also make powerful capabilities easier to redistribute or modify. Safety depends on the model, the safeguards, the deployment setting, the licence and the oversight process, not on the label alone.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: An open-weight model is a model whose trained settings have been shared so other people can run it themselves.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: An open-weight model is a trained machine-learning model for which the learned parameter values, usually checkpoint files containing weights, are publicly released for download and execution on compatible infrastructure. The release may permit inference, fine-tuning or further adaptation, depending on the licence and format. However, this does not imply release of the training dataset, data-cleaning pipeline, source code, architecture details beyond what can be inferred, optimiser state, evaluation suite, safety methods or unrestricted legal rights. In practice, 'open weight' describes the availability of a specific artefact in the model lifecycle, not complete openness of the whole system.

keyTakeaway: Open weights provide the trained parameter values, not necessarily the training data, code, full development record or unrestricted permission to use and adapt the model.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best describes an open-weight model?
options: A model whose weights are public, even if code, data or licence terms are not fully open
A model that always includes public training data and fully open-source code
A model that can only be used through the original company’s website
A model that has been proved accurate because many people can download it
quickCheck.explanation: The defining feature is release of the trained parameters. Other parts of the system may remain closed, partly described or legally restricted. Public availability also does not prove accuracy or safety.

searchKeywords: open weights vs open source ai
contested: The boundary of this term is genuinely unsettled. Many people use 'open-weight' narrowly to mean that trained weights are downloadable, while others expect some combination of code, documentation or permissive rights as well. The term is useful, but it does not by itself settle how open the overall system really is.

issues.problem: The result says the university can adapt the model because the weights were released. The scenario establishes permission for offline use and provides loading instructions, but it neither grants adaptation rights nor describes any adaptation. Releasing weights alone does not establish that adaptation is legally permitted.
issues.fix: The university can run the model locally because the weights and loading instructions were released, but it still depends on human review and may not have access to the original training data or full training pipeline.

issues.problem: The definition implies that releasing weights enables running or adaptation even when the licence is restrictive. Running also requires a compatible architecture and software, while adaptation may be prohibited by the licence.
issues.fix: A model whose trained numerical parameters are released for others to download, even if the training code and data are unavailable or the licence restricts use.

issues.problem: This again treats sharing weights as sufficient for running the model. Compatible architecture information, software and infrastructure are also required, and legal terms may restrict execution.
issues.fix: An open-weight model is a model whose trained settings are available for other people to download, subject to its format and licence.

issues.problem: The statement that a model can explain a judgment, merely less easily than a human clerk, presents generated explanations as faithful accounts of the model's computation. A generated rationale may not reflect why the output arose. The limitation also fails to expose the main structural mismatch: a readable scoring sheet has named, separable factors, while model behaviour arises from many interacting values.
issues.fix: A scoring sheet uses a few named factors whose effects can be read separately. Real model weights may contain millions or billions of interacting values, and no single value has the clear meaning of 'trust matching dates'. Running them also requires the matching architecture and software. The analogy shows that trained parameters can be shared without the training data, but it hides how model behaviour emerges from many interacting computations.

issues.problem: The visual mixes two different dimensions. Weights, code, data and methods can be marked by whether they are released, but a licence is described as restricted or permissive rather than released or not released. This contradicts the stated three-state legend and makes the comparison conceptually inconsistent.
issues.fix: Label the fifth row 'Usage rights'. Use released, partial and not released for artefacts. Use permissive, restricted and unclear for usage rights, with a separate legend.

issues.problem: Option 0 is the only defensible answer, but the distractors are so absolute and implausible that the answer is obvious without understanding the distinction. Option 1 says 'always' and 'fully', option 2 states the opposite of downloadable weights, and option 3 makes an unsupported proof claim.
issues.fix: Replace the options with: ["A model with downloadable weights, while its training data and some usage rights remain restricted", "A model with public code and architecture details, but no released trained weights", "A model accessed through an API that lets users request provider-run fine-tuning", "A model with published evaluations and parameter counts, but private checkpoint files"]. Keep correctOptionIndex as 0.

voicePass.note: Replaced generic scenarios with distinct workplace moments, strengthened the handling requirements for personal and procurement-sensitive material, and clarified the difference between released weights and a fully open system.
